script.title: Why Soldiers Signalled by Waving One Flag

lines: A Union captain kept signalling with a bedsheet as the enemy charged.
His signal began with an army surgeon, Albert J. Myer.
In 1851, Myer wrote a sign language for deaf people.
It tapped a code on a hand or cheek.
Posted to Texas, Myer turned those taps into the motions of one big flag.
Each letter was a quick set of dips, left or right.
In 1859, a board under Robert E. Lee saw only limited use for it.
But it let Myer keep testing.
You see, it's like waving to a friend across a field. A moving arm is easier to spot.
One flag meant both arms could raise a larger flag.
And motions are easier to tell apart than positions at great distances.
With a telescope, signalmen read stations up to 20 miles away.
Then the Civil War began.
Signalmen built towers, some well over 100 feet.
The Confederates sent a gun battery to destroy one. They failed.
At Gettysburg, the Confederates tried to seize Little Round Top.
Its flagman retreated with the flags.
Captain Davis E. Castle kept signalling with a bedsheet.
Myer never even called it wigwag.
The name probably came from how random the flag looked.

claims.claim: During Pickett's Charge one of the Union defenders, Captain Davis E. Castle, continued to signal with a bedsheet after the flagman had retreated with the flags; the Confederates had tried but failed to seize the Little Round Top position.
The wigwag system was invented by US Army surgeon Major Albert J. Myer in the 1850s.
In 1851 Myer produced A New Sign Language for Deaf Mutes, using the Bain code to communicate with a deaf person by tapping a hand or cheek.
In 1854 Myer joined the army, was posted to Texas, and there developed the wigwag flag code, building on his previous work with the deaf.
In 1859 a board of examination under Robert E. Lee thought it had only limited use but allowed Myer to continue with tests.
Only one flag is used, so both arms could raise a larger, heavier flag; motions are easier to distinguish than positions at great distances.
A telescope was used to read signals from a remote station up to 20 miles away.
Enormous towers, some well over 100 feet, were built; the Confederates assigned a gun battery to destroy the Cobb's Hill tower and failed.
Myer did not use the term wigwag; the name probably came from the apparently random motions of the flag as seen by an untrained observer.

cast.myer: a 30 year old American army surgeon, slim, a long oval face with a high forehead, wavy dark brown hair, a thick drooping dark moustache, wearing a dark blue army frock coat with brass buttons and green shoulder straps, 1850s
cast.castle: a 28 year old Union army captain, broad shouldered, a square clean-shaven jaw, short sandy blond hair, a dusty sweaty face, wearing a dark blue officer's coat open over a grey shirt and a dark blue kepi cap, 1860s
cast.signalman: a 19 year old Union private, skinny, a freckled narrow face, messy bright red hair, wearing a baggy dark blue sack coat, light blue trousers and a brown leather belt, 1860s
cast.deaf: a 35 year old American woman, a round friendly face, black hair parted in the middle in a low bun, wearing a mustard yellow cotton dress with a white collar, 1850s
